screens.title: Applying SRP: Practical Refactoring Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on practical ways to apply the Single Responsibility Principle to messy, real-world code. You will see how to find cohesive responsibilities inside a class, extract them into their own classes or interfaces, and recompose the system with dependency injection so each component has a single reason to change. You’ll also learn when composition is preferable to inheritance, and the safety precautions to make refactoring low risk: test coverage, small incremental steps, and the ‘‘reason to change’’ heuristic so you don’t over-engineer. By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify SRP violations, apply Extract Class and Extract Interface patterns, and refactor a UserService example while keeping external behavior unchanged. screens.title: Extract Class — What and Why
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Class is a refactoring that moves a cohesive set of methods and the data they use out of an existing class into a new class. The claim is simple: if a group of methods forms a distinct responsibility, they should live in their own class so the original class has one clear reason to change. A concrete example is taking validation logic and placing it in an OrderValidator class that exposes a validate method. That change makes unit testing and reuse straightforward — you test the validator independently and replace it if requirements change. A common misconception is to extract too eagerly: not every method pair that can be separated should be. Use the reason-to-change rule: extract when elements will change for different reasons. Another mistake is splitting without updating callers or adding tests; extract in one small step and run tests to ensure behavior remains unchanged. Key takeaway: Extract Class improves clarity, testability, and lowers cognitive load by making responsibilities explicit. Where in your code could a grouped set of methods form a focused new class? Extract Class — What and Why means move cohesive logic into a dedicated class so each class has a single responsibility and easier tests.. In practical terms, separate a cohesive set of methods and data into a new class with a single responsibility.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Extract Class
Definition & Rationale
Extract Class moves related methods and fields into a new class so each class has one reason to change. It reduces size and coupling of the original class and improves testability of the extracted logic.
When to extract
When methods and fields form a cohesive responsibility that could change for a different reason than the host class.
Common mistake
Extracting too granularly or without tests can increase complexity rather than reduce it.
Example card
Extract OrderValidator from OrderProcessor and test validation separately from persistence and email behavior.
Process — quick checklist
  1. Add or confirm tests for current behavior.
  2. Copy methods and relevant fields into a new class and make them private/protected as needed.
  3. Replace original logic with a delegation call to the new class and run tests.
  4. Refine constructors and dependencies, then commit when green.
Key Takeaway
Extract Class increases clarity and testability by grouping related behavior into a single-responsibility class. Verify with tests and small commits.

screens.title: Identify Extract Class Candidates
screens.narratorSegment: Finding a good Extract Class candidate is a detective task that combines code reading with change-history insight. Start by listing methods and fields in the large class and group them by purpose: validation, persistence, messaging, formatting, calculation, and so on. Next, consult version history or ask teammates to discover which groups change for different reasons. If a set of methods changes together while others change independently, that set is a strong candidate for extraction. Use the reason-to-change heuristic: ask, why would this group ever change separately from the rest? Create a small test that exercises that group’s behavior in isolation. If the test is straightforward, begin extraction in a single commit: move code to a new class, update callers to delegate, then run tests. A key misconception is thinking that all long classes must be split; some long classes are cohesive. The goal is to separate responsibilities that diverge in change frequency, not to create many tiny classes that always change together. What change history tells you about how code evolves is often the strongest signal. Identify Extract Class Candidates means group methods, consult change history, apply reason-to-change, write an isolated test, then extract in one step.. In practical terms, a step-by-step process to find responsibilities worth extracting.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Step-by-step
Use this short process to pick a safe candidate for Extract Class.

Group methods and fields

screens.title: Refactor: OrderProcessor → Collaborators
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows how to refactor a violating OrderProcessor into an orchestrator and focused collaborators. The original class performed validation, saving, emailing, inventory updates, and invoice generation in one method. The refactor extracts OrderValidator, OrderRepository, EmailService, InventoryService and InvoiceGenerator so OrderProcessor becomes an orchestrator. The pattern is straightforward: create the new collaborator classes with clear single-purpose methods, inject them into OrderProcessor via constructor parameters, then replace the inlined code with calls to those collaborators. This change makes each collaborator easy to unit test: for example, you can test EmailService independently or swap it for a mock when testing the orchestrator. A common misconception is that extraction always requires heavy architectural changes; often it’s simple delegation and dependency injection. Remember to add tests before extraction or run the test suite frequently after each small change. The closing question: after extracting, how will you mock and test each collaborator to keep integration tests minimal? content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › OrderProcessor Refactor
Original (simplified)
// Simplified
public class OrderProcessor {
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // 1. validate
        // 2. save to DB
        // 3. send email
        // 4. update inventory
        // 5. generate invoice
    }
}
This single method mixes many responsibilities and is hard to test in isolation.
Refactored orchestration
public class OrderProcessor {
    private OrderValidator validator;
    private OrderRepository repository;
    private EmailService emailService;
    private InventoryService inventoryService;
    private InvoiceGenerator invoiceGenerator;

    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        validator.validate(order);
        repository.save(order);
        emailService.sendConfirmationEmail(order.getCustomerEmail(), order.getId());
        inventoryService.updateInventory(order.getItems());
        invoiceGenerator.generatePdf(order);
    }
}
OrderProcessor now coordinates collaborators that each have a single responsibility and can be tested independently.
Key Takeaway
Replace internal responsibilities with collaborators and delegate. This keeps behavior the same while improving structure.

screens.title: Extract Interface — Define Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Interface is a refactoring that yields an interface declaring the minimal methods required for a responsibility. The primary benefit is loose coupling: other classes depend on the interface rather than a concrete implementation. For example, creating an IEmailSender interface with a sendEmail method allows you to implement a production SMTP sender and a lightweight MockEmailService for tests. This makes the orchestrating class depend only on the contract it needs, enabling easier substitution and following the Open/Closed Principle. A frequent misconception is that interfaces add overhead; in practice they simplify testing and future changes because implementations can be swapped without touching callers. When designing an interface, include only what collaborators need — avoid exposing implementation details. Also prefer descriptive names and keep interfaces small and focused so they match single responsibilities. The closing question: what behaviors in your codebase would become easier to test if an interface were extracted? Extract Interface — Define Contracts means create small interfaces to declare required behavior and let callers depend on contracts, not implementations.. In practical terms, use interfaces to declare only the methods needed for a responsibility.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Extract Interface
Minimal contract
Define an interface that exposes only the operations clients need.
public interface IEmailSender {
    void sendEmail(String recipient, String subject, String body);
}

public class SmtpEmailService implements IEmailSender { ... }
public class MockEmailService implements IEmailSender { ... }
Benefits
  • Loose coupling: swap implementations without changing callers.
  • Testability: inject mocks or fakes in unit tests.
  • Clarity: callers express their dependencies via interfaces.
Avoid adding every method from a concrete class; keep the interface focused on the single responsibility it represents.

screens.title: Composition over Inheritance
screens.narratorSegment: Composition and inheritance are both ways to reuse behavior, but they have different trade-offs for SRP. Inheritance creates an 'is-a' relationship and can force subclasses to carry methods and data they don't need, which can violate single responsibility. For example, if Vehicle has a refuel method, ElectricCar as a subclass must provide an awkward implementation or an empty override. Composition avoids that by giving objects collaborators that handle specific responsibilities: a Vehicle can have an IPowerSource. Then GasolineEngine and ElectricMotor implement IPowerSource. The advantage is flexibility: you can change the engine at runtime or provide test doubles easily. A common misconception is that inheritance is simpler; for domain models with orthogonal concerns, composition yields clearer separation of responsibilities and easier testing. The practical takeaway is to prefer composition unless you have a true 'is-a' relationship that aligns with responsibilities. Where has inheritance led to awkward overrides in your codebase? Composition over Inheritance means use composition to assemble focused collaborators and avoid subclasses inheriting unrelated responsibilities.. In practical terms, why 'has-a' is often better than 'is-a' for managing responsibilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Composition vs Inheritance
Inheritance example
Vehicle with drive and refuel. ElectricCar may not refuel in the same way, leading to awkward overrides or empty methods.
Pitfall: subclasses inherit responsibilities they don't need, increasing coupling and violating SRP.
Composition example
Vehicle has an IPowerSource. Implement GasolineEngine or ElectricMotor and inject into Vehicle. Each power source has a single responsibility.
Benefit: swap behaviors at runtime, simpler tests, clearer SRP alignment.

screens.title: Refactor Safely: Tests, Steps, and Commits
screens.narratorSegment: Safe refactoring is about preserving observable behavior while improving internal structure. Start by ensuring you have adequate automated tests that capture the behavior of the code you intend to change. If tests are missing, write focused tests before editing. Then refactor in tiny steps: extract one responsibility, run tests, commit, and repeat. Use dependency injection to replace concrete dependencies with mocks or fakes during testing. A common pitfall is attempting a large refactor in a single edit; this makes rollbacks and bug isolation difficult. Another mistake is forgetting integration tests for the orchestration logic; unit tests are necessary but not always sufficient. Keep your commits atomic and descriptive so you can bisect if a regression appears. Finally, don’t over-extract: apply the reason-to-change heuristic to avoid creating classes that will always change together. The closing question: which small refactor could you do safely this afternoon with your current test suite? In practical terms, how to keep behavior identical while changing structure.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Refactor Safety
Minimal safety checklist
  • Have tests that fail when behavior changes incorrectly.
  • Refactor one responsibility per commit.
  • Use DI to inject test doubles where needed.
  • Run unit and relevant integration tests after each change.
Practical tips
If a change causes many test failures, revert and split the change into smaller steps. Keep commits small and descriptive so the history documents intent.
Key Takeaway: A green test suite plus small atomic commits is your safety net during refactoring.

screens.title: Don't Over-Engineer: Reason-to-Change Heuristic
screens.narratorSegment: A persistent trap during refactoring is over-engineering: creating tiny classes for every line of code rather than grouping logically coherent responsibilities. The reason-to-change heuristic helps avoid this: two pieces of code should be in separate classes only if they are likely to change for different reasons. Consider calculatePrice and displayProductDetails: if price calculation changes with tax rules while display markup changes with UI needs, they have different reasons to change and should be separated. Conversely, if two methods always evolve together, splitting them only increases indirection. Another misconception is that more classes always mean better design; the real goal is maintainability and clarity. Use tests and small commits to evaluate if the split improves readability and reduces coupling. When in doubt, extract, run tests, and observe whether the change simplified the code paths and testing. The reflective question: will extracting this part make future changes easier or just add ceremony? Don't Over-Engineer: Reason-to-Change Heuristic means only extract when the components will change for different reasons; avoid needless fragmentation.. In practical terms, extract only when parts have different reasons to change.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Reason-to-Change

Ask: would this code change for different reasons than the rest? If yes, extract. If not, keep together.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on practical ways to apply the Single Responsibility Principle to messy, real-world code. You will see how to find cohesive responsibilities inside a class, extract them into their own classes or interfaces, and recompose the system with dependency injection so each component has a single reason to change. We will walk through a running example — an OrderProcessor that mixes validation, persistence, email sending, inventory and invoice generation — and refactor it into clear collaborators. You’ll also learn when composition is preferable to inheritance, and the safety precautions to make refactoring low risk: test coverage, small incremental steps, and the ‘‘reason to change’’ heuristic so you don’t over-engineer. By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify SRP violations, apply Extract Class and Extract Interface patterns, and refactor a UserService example while keeping external behavior unchanged. Think about an example from your codebase where a single class does dozens of things; this lesson shows how to split it into replaceable, testable parts.

In this session you will master a set of concrete refactoring skills that apply SRP in existing code. First, you’ll learn how to use Extract Class to split a monolithic class into focused collaborators so each class has one responsibility and one reason to change. Second, you will practice Extract Interface to define stable contracts for those responsibilities, which enables loose coupling and easier testing. Third, you will learn to prefer composition over inheritance so behaviors can be swapped without fragile hierarchies. Finally, you will apply these techniques in a hands-on UserService refactor where password hashing and persistence are moved into separate components. Each objective is paired with a visual mnemonic or micro-check to help you decide when to extract. We’ll also include a verified competency milestone so you know when you can consider an objective mastered. These skills are practical and directly applicable the next time you encounter a sprawling class in your codebase.

This second objectives screen focuses on practice: how to execute and verify each refactor. For Extract Class, practice by identifying a set of methods and fields that change together, extract them, and run tests. A concrete example is moving password hashing into a PasswordHasher class, then asserting user creation behavior remains unchanged. For Extract Interface, write an interface for persistence or email sending, then inject a mock implementation during tests to confirm loose coupling. When exercising composition over inheritance, refactor a tight hierarchy into a composed set of collaborators and run integration tests to confirm behavior. Each objective includes a verified milestone: a passing test suite demonstrating identical external behavior after the change. That test-first rhythm gives you confidence to refactor in small steps. Use the reason-to-change heuristic: don’t split code just to split; split when parts will change for different reasons. These practices keep refactors safe and pragmatic.

Extract Class is a refactoring that moves a cohesive set of methods and the data they use out of an existing class into a new class. The claim is simple: if a group of methods forms a distinct responsibility, they should live in their own class so the original class has one clear reason to change. A concrete example is taking validation logic and placing it in an OrderValidator class that exposes a validate method. That change makes unit testing and reuse straightforward — you test the validator independently and replace it if requirements change. A common misconception is to extract too eagerly: not every method pair that can be separated should be. Use the reason-to-change rule: extract when elements will change for different reasons. Another mistake is splitting without updating callers or adding tests; extract in one small step and run tests to ensure behavior remains unchanged. Key takeaway: Extract Class improves clarity, testability, and lowers cognitive load by making responsibilities explicit. Where in your code could a grouped set of methods form a focused new class? Extract Class — What and Why means move cohesive logic into a dedicated class so each class has a single responsibility and easier tests.. In practical terms, separate a cohesive set of methods and data into a new class with a single responsibility.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Finding a good Extract Class candidate is a detective task that combines code reading with change-history insight. Start by listing methods and fields in the large class and group them by purpose: validation, persistence, messaging, formatting, calculation, and so on. Next, consult version history or ask teammates to discover which groups change for different reasons. If a set of methods changes together while others change independently, that set is a strong candidate for extraction. Use the reason-to-change heuristic: ask, why would this group ever change separately from the rest? Create a small test that exercises that group’s behavior in isolation. If the test is straightforward, begin extraction in a single commit: move code to a new class, update callers to delegate, then run tests. A key misconception is thinking that all long classes must be split; some long classes are cohesive. The goal is to separate responsibilities that diverge in change frequency, not to create many tiny classes that always change together. What change history tells you about how code evolves is often the strongest signal. This walkthrough shows how to refactor a violating OrderProcessor into an orchestrator and focused collaborators. The original class performed validation, saving, emailing, inventory updates, and invoice generation in one method. The refactor extracts OrderValidator, OrderRepository, EmailService, InventoryService and InvoiceGenerator so OrderProcessor becomes an orchestrator. The pattern is straightforward: create the new collaborator classes with clear single-purpose methods, inject them into OrderProcessor via constructor parameters, then replace the inlined code with calls to those collaborators. Extract Interface is a refactoring that yields an interface declaring the minimal methods required for a responsibility. The primary benefit is loose coupling: other classes depend on the interface rather than a concrete implementation. Composition and inheritance are both ways to reuse behavior, but they have different trade-offs for SRP. In summary, Extract Class moves cohesive logic into a new class so each class has a single reason to change. Extract Interface defines a minimal contract so callers depend on behavior rather than concrete implementations, enabling easy substitution and testing. Prefer composition over inheritance for responsibilities that vary independently, using injected collaborators rather than forcing subclasses to carry unrelated methods. Safety comes from tests, incremental commits, and the reason-to-change heuristic: extract only when parts will change for different reasons. Together these practices make code more modular, testable, and easier to evolve.
